For years, the race to build better artificial intelligence centered on making models bigger, feeding them more data, and expanding the amount of information they could process at once. Now, a fresh frontier is emerging as researchers increasingly explore smarter memory management as another way to build more capable AI systems. Two academic papers published this month, AutoMem and SelfMem, argue that memory shouldn't be a rigid feature engineered by developers using static rules. Instead, they propose that AI systems can learn to manage their own memories. They take different approaches: AutoMem trains AI to manage an external memory system, while SelfMem lets agents refine their own memory strategies through feedback, and both report substantial gains on long-horizon benchmarks. Imagine working with an AI coding assistant on a project for months. Instead of repeatedly reminding it about your project's architecture and coding style, a smarter memory system could retain the decisions that matter while discarding obsolete information. Researchers believe that this kind of selective memory will become increasingly important as AI agents take on longer-running tasks. One way developers have tried to build more capable chatbots is by expanding their context windows, which are the immediate digital scratchpad an AI considers during a conversation. While larger context windows let models process more information, they also increase computational costs and don't necessarily help AI distinguish useful information from irrelevant details. The papers instead explore an alternative approach based on active memory curation. In AutoMem, Stanford University researchers introduced a memory manager that decides when to create, update, search, and delete records, allowing the AI to maintain a compact memory instead of continuously accumulating information. Tested on grueling, complex video games like NetHack and Crafter, this memory-management approach slashed the agent's memory growth rate by 95% and doubled its task performance, allowing a 32-billion-parameter open-weight model to perform competitively with frontier models including Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Thinking on the evaluated long-horizon benchmarks. SelfMem takes a completely parameter-free approach. Instead of editing model weights, it gives the AI a dedicated workspace and tools to inspect an unchangeable transcript store. It allows the agent to inspect, write, review, and revise its own memory, outperforming traditional retrieval pipelines by more than 40% on the BEAM benchmark while using only a fraction of the computational cost. The push for smarter memory comes as AI companies shift from one-off chatbots to autonomous agents designed to work over days or weeks. Whether writing software, tracking supply chains, or managing research projects, these systems must retain relevant information while discarding details that no longer matter. That is where autonomous memory management changes the equation. Instead of forcing a user to repeatedly copy-paste instructions, an agent equipped with an optimized memory workflow seamlessly recalls structural boundaries, tracks cumulative progress, and discards transient data that is no longer relevant. Better memory could also reduce the computational cost of repeatedly processing the same information, a potential advantage as AI companies look to deploy agents more efficiently at scale. Over the past year, leading AI companies like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic have introduced basic memory features, allowing consumer chatbots to retain user preferences and custom instructions across distinct chat sessions. Today's commercial memory features generally rely on predefined mechanisms for deciding what information is retained. AutoMem and SelfMem instead point toward AI systems capable of independently evaluating and regulating their own memories. As tech companies race to build AI systems capable of executing truly long-horizon work, the findings suggest memory management may become an increasingly important complement to larger models. Future AI systems may be judged not only by how much they know, but also by how effectively they decide what information is worth keeping. As the market's fears of an artificial intelligence (AI) bubble grow, investors would be well advised to focus on companies that have real earnings, durable competitive advantages, and exposure to long-term demand. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM) stands out for its dominance in chip manufacturing, making it one of the strongest stocks to hold even if the AI hype fades. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Chipmakers like Nvidia and AMD continue to design processors capable of handling ever more demanding computing workloads. What most of the designers don't do is manufacture them in-house. Churning out high-end chips at scale requires specialized technology, expertise, and foundries that are neither cheap nor easy to build. That's where Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing comes in. TSM runs the world's largest third-party foundry business, manufacturing chips designed by its customers for use not only in AI, but also in smartphones and other electronics. It's one of the few that has the technological capability to produce the advanced, transistor-dense chips that power the AI industry, so essentially all of the leading designers make use of its services. As a result, TSM's success is not tied to the success of any single AI application or chip designer. This business model gives TSM shareholders broad exposure to the AI race, and spares them from having to predict which chip designers will emerge as its biggest winners. That advantage will matter even more if and when investor sentiment toward the sector turns sour. Even if the market begins to question the valuations of individual AI stocks, demand for chip manufacturing could remain strong as businesses continue to develop and deploy compute-heavy technologies. That said, TSM would not be immune to an AI sector downturn. If data center customers and other chip-using businesses cut their spending or delay orders, the foundry giant could feel the effects. TSM also faces geopolitical risks because its manufacturing base is concentrated in Taiwan, where a conflict with China could disrupt production. Graphics processing units (GPUs) are essential to training and running AI models. But as AI systems become more advanced, demand for compute power is spreading across several chip categories. Agentic AI workloads, for example, require data centers to have a larger proportion of central processing units (CPUs). And hyperscalers are also designing and deploying larger numbers of application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) that are custom-built to handle their AI workloads. TSM is well positioned to benefit from this diversifying demand because it manufactures all of those types of chips. If AI adoption continues to expand into enterprise software, consumer devices, and other applications, chip demand could remain healthy even if investor sentiment toward top AI companies weakens. TSM doesn't need every AI application to succeed; it just needs enough customers to keep investing in advanced chips. Beyond the chips themselves, TSM is also investing heavily in its manufacturing technology. It began volume production using its 2-nanometer (2nm) process node in the fourth quarter of 2025. But the company continues to improve its manufacturing technology, with volume production for its N2P and A16 nodes ramping up in the second half of 2026. Its longer-term roadmap includes the even more powerful A14 process node, which is expected to enter volume production in 2028. These steady advancements are important because AI developers demand chips that can deliver more compute without letting power consumption and operating costs spiral out of control. For investors worried about how long the AI boom can last, TSM's roadmap offers a reason to look beyond short-term sentiment. The company is investing in manufacturing capabilities to support future generations of advanced chips, rather than relying on a single product cycle, which makes TSM much more resilient to cracks in the AI bubble. But how do analysts and the valuation view the stock? Wall Street remains bullish on TSM: Among 19 analysts covering the stock, 16 rate it a strong buy, two a buy, and just one a hold. Their average price target, meanwhile, suggests 23% potential upside over the next year. And based on its current price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of over 27, investors are expecting AI-driven chip demand to continue fueling growth. The company's manufacturing expertise and strong position in the AI supply chain give it a compelling long-term bull case. With that, TSM may be one of the strongest ways to invest in AI, even if fears that the sector is in a bubble intensify.
